questions.question: When would you choose a message queue (RabbitMQ) over an event stream (Kafka)? What are the trade-offs?
questions.title: Message Queues vs Event Streams: RabbitMQ vs Kafka Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: **Message queues** (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, SQS) are designed for **task delivery** — each message is processed by one consumer and then deleted; the broker tracks state, supports complex routing (topic exchanges, headers), and gives priority/delay/dead-letter queues out of the box. **Event streams** (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis) are designed for **event log persistence** — messages stay on the log indefinitely, multiple consumer groups read independently at their own offsets, and the log can be replayed. Pick a **queue for task processing** (image transcoding, sending emails, RPC over messaging). Pick a **stream for event distribution** (CDC, audit logs, analytics pipelines, multiple consumers needing the same events).

interviewer_intent.testing: Fundamental difference between push-based queue and pull-based log, ordering guarantees, replay capability, and consumer-group semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Kafka as a 'better RabbitMQ' (it's not — different patterns) or assuming queues can replay messages.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss ordering guarantees per partition vs per queue, exactly-once semantics, retention policies, and modern blurring (RabbitMQ Streams, SQS FIFO).

sections.title: Two Different Mental Models
sections.content:
**Message queue — the post office model.**
- Producer drops a letter; broker delivers it to one consumer; consumer processes it; broker discards.
- The broker holds state about which message went to which consumer.
- Once delivered and acked, the message is gone.
- Routing is rich: topic exchanges, headers, fanout, direct.

**Event stream — the newspaper / append-only log model.**
- Producer appends an event to the log; the log is immutable and persistent.
- Many consumer groups can read the same log independently, each at its own position (offset).
- Events stay on disk for days/weeks/forever, regardless of who has read them.
- Routing is simpler (topic + partition); the magic is in the log shape.

The two solve different problems and live happily side by side in modern stacks.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Message Queue (RabbitMQ) | Event Stream (Kafka) |
|---|---|---|
| Storage model | Per-message state in broker; deleted after ack | Immutable append-only log; retention in days/weeks |
| Delivery | Push to consumer | Consumer pulls at own pace |
| Ordering | Per-queue (with single consumer) | Per-partition |
| Replay | No (once acked, gone) | Yes (read from any offset) |
| Consumers | Each message goes to one consumer in a queue | Each consumer group reads the full log independently |
| Throughput | ~10-50K msg/sec per node | ~1M+ msg/sec per cluster |
| Latency | Low (sub-ms broker latency) | Slightly higher (5-15ms typical) |
| Routing | Rich (exchanges, headers, topic) | Simple (topic + partition key) |
| Priorities | Yes (message priority queues) | No native (use multiple topics) |
| Delay/scheduled | Yes (TTL + DLX trick or plugins) | No native (workarounds) |
| Dead-letter | Native | App-level (separate topic) |
| Backpressure | Slow consumers cause queue growth (broker memory pressure) | Slow consumers fall behind (lag); broker unaffected |

sections.title: When to Use a Message Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, ActiveMQ)
sections.content:
**Task processing pipelines.** Image resize, email sending, PDF generation, video transcoding kickoff. Workers pull from the queue, process, ack. If a worker crashes, the queue redelivers.

**Request/response with backpressure.** RPC over messaging; the broker absorbs spikes when workers are slow.

**Complex routing.** 'Send this message to all subscribers matching `topic.usa.*`'. RabbitMQ's topic exchange does this elegantly; Kafka would need many topics or smart consumer code.

**Priority and scheduling.** Premium customers' jobs run first; this email goes out in 24 hours. Native in queues; awkward in streams.

**Per-message lifecycle.** You care about *this individual task* — ack it, redeliver it, dead-letter it.

**Examples:**
- Sidekiq (Redis), Celery (RabbitMQ), AWS SQS-based job processing.
- Internal service-to-service RPC where you want async + buffering.
- Email and notification dispatch.

sections.title: When to Use an Event Stream (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis)
sections.content:
**Event distribution to many consumers.** A `user.signup` event needs to update analytics, send a welcome email, feed the recommendation model, populate the CRM. With Kafka, each consumer group reads independently — add a new consumer next year, replay from the beginning.

**Change Data Capture (CDC).** Database changes streamed to downstream consumers (search index, cache invalidation, data warehouse). Debezium → Kafka is the canonical pattern.

**Event sourcing / audit logs.** Append-only event history is the source of truth; views are projections.

**Analytics pipelines.** Stream click events through Kafka → Spark / Flink → dashboards. Replay if the analytics job has a bug.

**Very high throughput.** Kafka's design (sequential disk writes, zero-copy, batching) handles millions of events/sec. RabbitMQ tops out an order of magnitude lower.

**Stream processing.** Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming all assume an event log shape.

**Examples:**
- LinkedIn invented Kafka for activity stream feeds.
- Uber routes 4 trillion+ messages per day through Kafka.
- Stripe uses Kafka for payment event distribution.
- Netflix pipes everything through Kafka for the data platform.

sections.title: Architecture Diagrams
sections.content:
**Queue (RabbitMQ):** ```mermaid flowchart LR P1[Producer 1] P2[Producer 2] Ex{Exchange
topic / direct} Q1[Queue: emails] Q2[Queue: images] C1[Worker 1] C2[Worker 2] C3[Worker 3] DLQ[Dead Letter
Queue] P1 --> Ex P2 --> Ex Ex -->|routing key: email.*| Q1 Ex -->|routing key: image.*| Q2 Q1 --> C1 Q1 --> C2 Q2 --> C3 Q1 -.failed messages.-> DLQ ``` Messages from each queue go to *one* of the workers connected to that queue. **Stream (Kafka):** ```mermaid flowchart LR P1[Producer 1] P2[Producer 2] Topic[(Topic: events
partitions 0,1,2)] CG1[Consumer Group:
analytics] CG2[Consumer Group:
email] CG3[Consumer Group:
warehouse] P1 --> Topic P2 --> Topic Topic --> CG1 Topic --> CG2 Topic --> CG3 ``` Each consumer group reads the *entire* event stream independently. Within a group, partitions are split among instances.

sections.title: Ordering, Delivery, and Exactly-Once
sections.content:
**Ordering:**
- **Queue:** order preserved per queue when there's a single consumer. With multiple consumers (parallel), order is lost across messages.
- **Stream:** order preserved **per partition**. A 'user-id' partition key guarantees all events for that user land in one partition, in order.

**Delivery semantics:**
- **At-most-once:** broker delivers once; if consumer fails, message is lost. Rare.
- **At-least-once (default):** broker redelivers on consumer failure; consumer might see duplicates. Both queues and streams default here.
- **Exactly-once:** dedupe at consumer (idempotency keys) or use broker-supported transactions.
  - Kafka: transactional producer + read-process-write atomic offsets.
  - RabbitMQ: harder to achieve; usually app-level idempotency.

**The reality:** even with 'exactly-once' broker support, end-to-end exactly-once requires idempotent consumers. Plan for at-least-once and dedupe.

**Backpressure:**
- **Queue:** slow consumers → queue grows in broker memory → broker pressure.
- **Stream:** slow consumers → consumer lag (offset behind log head) → broker unaffected; producers keep producing.

sections.title: Operational Concerns
sections.content:
**RabbitMQ ops:**
- Mirror queues across nodes for HA.
- Watch for queue sprawl (one consumer = one queue = lots of metadata).
- Memory pressure if consumers fall behind — spillover to disk slows everything.
- Cluster network partitions: tricky; use 'pause_minority' policy.

**Kafka ops:**
- Partition count is the unit of parallelism per consumer group; pick carefully (changing later requires rebalancing).
- Replication factor 3, min ISR 2 for HA.
- Consumer lag is the key metric — alert when lag exceeds N seconds of producer rate.
- Disk-heavy: the log is the data; size the cluster for retention × throughput.
- Zookeeper or KRaft for metadata.

**Cost:**
- Kafka requires more disk (long retention) but scales horizontally.
- RabbitMQ is lighter for low-volume, simple-routing setups.
- Managed services: AWS MSK / Confluent Cloud (Kafka), AWS MQ / CloudAMQP (RabbitMQ); pick based on team familiarity.

sections.title: When the Lines Blur
sections.content:
**RabbitMQ Streams (3.9+):** RabbitMQ added an append-only log similar to Kafka. Replay support. Same broker, two abstractions.

**Kafka with short retention (1 hour):** behaves more like a distributed queue if you only have one consumer group. But you lose the 'multi-consumer replay' benefit.

**SQS FIFO + dedup:** SQS now offers per-message-group ordering and content-based dedup, narrowing the gap.

**Pulsar:** unifies queue and stream semantics in one product (per-subscription mode chooses behavior).

**Practical guidance:** the tool name matters less than the **pattern you need**. Ask:
- Do multiple independent consumers need the same data? → Stream.
- Is replay valuable? → Stream.
- Is per-message lifecycle (ack/redeliver/DLQ) the value? → Queue.
- Is throughput ≥ 100K msg/sec? → Stream.
- Is rich routing (topic patterns, headers) needed? → Queue.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Queue = one consumer per message, deleted after ack;** rich routing, priorities, delays, DLQ.
- **Stream = persistent log, many consumer groups, replay;** higher throughput, partition-based ordering.
- **Ordering:** per-queue (queue) vs per-partition (stream); pick partition key wisely.
- **At-least-once is the realistic default;** make consumers idempotent.
- **Use queues for task processing;** use streams for event distribution, CDC, analytics.
- **Modern brokers blur the line** — RabbitMQ Streams, SQS FIFO, Pulsar.
- **Pick by pattern, not by brand familiarity.**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two different mental models**

Message queue is the post-office model: producer drops a letter, broker delivers to one consumer, consumer processes, broker discards. Per-message state in the broker. Rich routing.

Event stream is the newspaper model: producer appends to an immutable log, the log persists for days/weeks, many consumer groups read independently at their own offsets. Replay any time.

**When to use a queue — RabbitMQ, SQS, ActiveMQ**

- Task processing: image resize, email sending, video transcoding kickoff
- RPC over messaging with backpressure
- Complex routing: topic exchanges, headers, fanout
- Priorities and scheduled delivery: premium customers first, send in 24h
- Per-message lifecycle: this individual task — ack, redeliver, dead-letter

**When to use a stream — Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis**

- Event distribution to many consumers: user.signup → analytics + email + recommendations + CRM, each as separate consumer groups
- Change Data Capture (Debezium → Kafka)
- Event sourcing and audit logs as source of truth
- Analytics pipelines (clickstream → Kafka → Flink → dashboards) with replay if jobs have bugs
- Very high throughput — Kafka does millions of events/sec; RabbitMQ tops out around 50K
- Stream processing (Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming)

**Ordering and delivery**

Queue: order preserved per queue with one consumer; lost across multiple parallel consumers.
Stream: order preserved per partition. Partition key like user-id keeps all events for one user in order in one partition.

Delivery defaults to at-least-once for both. Exactly-once is achievable with broker support (Kafka transactions) but realistically you make consumers idempotent and accept duplicates.

Backpressure differs:
- Queue: slow consumers grow the queue in broker memory — broker pressure
- Stream: slow consumers fall behind (consumer lag) but broker is unaffected; producers keep producing

**Operations**

RabbitMQ: mirror queues for HA, watch queue sprawl, memory pressure if consumers fall behind, network partitions need pause-minority policy.

Kafka: partition count = unit of parallelism per consumer group, pick carefully; replication factor 3, min ISR 2; consumer lag is THE metric; disk-heavy because the log is the data.

Cost: Kafka heavier disk + ops, RabbitMQ lighter for low-volume; managed options (MSK, Confluent Cloud, AWS MQ, CloudAMQP) reduce ops burden either way.

**Modern blurring**

- RabbitMQ Streams: log abstraction inside RabbitMQ
- SQS FIFO + content-based dedup: narrows the gap
- Pulsar: per-subscription mode chooses queue or stream behavior

**Decision questions**

Do multiple independent consumers need the same data? → Stream
Is replay valuable? → Stream
Is per-message ack/redeliver/DLQ the value? → Queue
≥ 100K msg/sec? → Stream
Need rich routing (topic patterns, headers)? → Queue

**Recommendation**

**RabbitMQ for task queues with rich routing, priorities, scheduled delivery, and per-message lifecycle. Kafka for event distribution where multiple downstream consumers need the same data, for CDC, audit logs, analytics pipelines, and any throughput above 100K msg/sec. They live happily side by side in modern stacks — use both for what each does best, not as substitutes for each other.**

When would Pulsar be a better choice than Kafka or RabbitMQ?
How do you handle a consumer that's an order of magnitude slower than the producer?
Design an event-driven order pipeline using Kafka. How many topics, what partitioning?

questions.question: How do you design an audit log system? When should you use Event Sourcing?
questions.title: Audit Log Design and Event Sourcing
questions.direct_answer: An **audit log** is an append-only record of significant actions — who did what, when, with what payload, and what was the result. Implement with **immutable rows** (PostgreSQL append-only tables, S3 with object lock, or Kafka) plus a **separate read model** for queries (Elasticsearch by user/time/object). **Event Sourcing** is the next step — the event log becomes the **source of truth** for application state; current state is rebuilt by replaying events. Use plain audit logging for compliance and 'who-did-what'; reach for full Event Sourcing only when you need **temporal queries, perfect history, or undo/redo** — it's powerful but adds significant complexity (snapshots, projections, event-versioning).

interviewer_intent.testing: Audit log requirements (immutability, signing, retention, queryability), separation of write log from read views, and understanding of Event Sourcing as a pattern.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in the audit writer (couples audit to logic), or claiming Event Sourcing is 'just keeping a log' (it's a much deeper pattern with projections, snapshots, replay).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss tamper-evidence (hash chains, signed events), event versioning + upcasting, snapshots for rebuild speed, and CQRS as the natural fit for ES.

sections.title: Audit Log Requirements
sections.content:
An audit log captures every action that matters — for compliance, security forensics, debugging, and user-visible activity feeds. Requirements:

- **Immutable** — once written, never modified or deleted.
- **Comprehensive** — captures actor, action, timestamp, target object, before/after state, request metadata (IP, user agent).
- **Tamper-evident** — you can detect if someone modified the log (hash chain, signing).
- **Queryable** — 'show me all changes by user X to object Y in the last 7 days.'
- **Retained per policy** — GDPR may say 7 years for some events; SOC2/HIPAA have their own rules.
- **Performant** — the audit write must not slow down the action it's auditing.

Which is harder than it sounds: append-only at one consistency level + queryable across many dimensions usually means **two storage tiers** (write log + read index).

sections.title: Audit Log Schema
sections.content:
```
audit_events
── event_id           UUID PRIMARY KEY
── occurred_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL  -- when the action happened
── recorded_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL  -- when we wrote it (for skew detection)
── actor_type         VARCHAR(20)            -- USER, SYSTEM, API_KEY
── actor_id           VARCHAR(100)
── action             VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL  -- USER_LOGIN, ORDER_CREATED, ROLE_GRANTED
── target_type        VARCHAR(50)            -- order, user, document
── target_id          VARCHAR(100)
── before_value       JSONB                  -- previous state snapshot (optional)
── after_value        JSONB                  -- new state snapshot (optional)
── metadata           JSONB                  -- IP, user-agent, request-id, geo
── outcome            VARCHAR(20)            -- SUCCESS, FAILED, DENIED
── prev_hash          BYTEA                  -- hash chain pointer
── hash               BYTEA                  -- hash of this row + prev_hash
```

**Immutability enforcement:**
- PostgreSQL: trigger-based (`BEFORE UPDATE`/`DELETE` raise exception) or `INSERT-only` role.
- S3: object lock with retention period.
- Kafka: log compaction disabled; retention policy = forever.
- Append-only ledger DBs: AWS QLDB, immudb.

sections.title: Tamper-Evidence — Hash Chain and Signing
sections.content:
**Hash chain (blockchain-lite):**
- Each event's `hash = SHA256(prev_hash || event_payload)`.
- Tampering with any historical event invalidates all subsequent hashes.
- Periodically publish the latest hash to an external write-only store or sign + email it (e.g., publish daily to a S3 bucket with object lock).

**Signed events:**
- Each event signed with the writer's private key.
- Verifies origin and integrity at any time.
- Adds CPU cost; reserve for high-stakes audit (financial, security).

**External notarization:**
- Periodic Merkle root committed to an immutable external store (AWS QLDB, blockchain, signed S3 object).
- Strongest tamper-evidence; legal-grade.

For most enterprise audit logs, hash chain + immutable storage is enough; full notarization is for regulated industries (banks, healthcare).

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB App[Application Services] Bus[Kafka
audit-events topic] Writer[Audit Writer
service] Cold[(Append-only Log
Postgres / S3 / QLDB)] Indexer[Indexer] Search[(Elasticsearch
by user/time/object)] UI[Audit UI / API] App -->|publish event| Bus Bus --> Writer Writer -->|append + hash| Cold Bus --> Indexer Indexer --> Search UI --> Search UI -.detail fetch.-> Cold classDef bus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b classDef store fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444 classDef svc fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e class Bus bus class Cold,Search store class App,Writer,Indexer,UI svc ``` **Why two stores:** - **Cold log** (Postgres / S3 / QLDB): immutable, hash-chained, source of truth. Optimized for append + sequential scan, not random query. - **Search index** (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch): denormalized, queryable by user, time, target, action. Rebuildable from the cold log. Queries hit the search index; if a user clicks 'show full payload,' the UI fetches the detailed row from cold storage by event_id.

sections.title: Writing Audit Events Reliably
sections.content:
**The hard part:** the audit must be written if and only if the action succeeded — no orphan audits and no missing audits.

**Pattern 1: Outbox.**
- App writes the business change AND the audit event to its own DB in the same transaction.
- A separate worker reads the outbox table and publishes to Kafka.
- Atomic w.r.t. business logic; eventually consistent w.r.t. audit pipeline.

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE id = ?;
INSERT INTO outbox (event) VALUES ('OrderShipped...');
COMMIT;
```

**Pattern 2: CDC (Debezium → Kafka).**
- Listen to the database WAL; produce events to Kafka automatically.
- No explicit publish in code; pure data-driven.
- Used heavily for cross-cutting audit + replication.

**Pattern 3: Direct dual-write (anti-pattern).**
- App writes to DB, then publishes to Kafka.
- Risk: app crashes between the two → missing audit.
- Don't do this; use outbox or CDC.

**Backpressure / failure isolation:**
- Audit pipeline must not block the user's action.
- If Kafka is down, outbox table buffers writes; worker drains when Kafka recovers.

sections.title: Now — What Is Event Sourcing
sections.content:
Event Sourcing (ES) takes the audit log idea further: **the event log IS the source of truth.** No 'current state' table is authoritative; current state is *derived* by replaying events.

**Plain audit log:**
- `orders` table holds current state.
- `audit_events` table holds the change history (separate, secondary).
- If audit log is lost, business still works.

**Event Sourcing:**
- `order_events` table is the only persistence (`OrderCreated`, `ItemAdded`, `Shipped`, `Cancelled`).
- Current order state is `fold(events)` — replay all events to compute it.
- 'Current state' tables (read models) are projections; rebuildable from events.
- If a read model is corrupted, drop it and rebuild from events.

**The benefits:**
- **Perfect history.** You know exactly what happened and when.
- **Time travel.** Reconstruct state as of any past moment.
- **New views for free.** Want a new dashboard? Project from events.
- **Bug fixes via replay.** Fix the projection logic, replay events.
- **Natural fit for CQRS** — events are the C side; projections are the Q side.

**The costs:**
- Schema evolution is hard (events are immutable but their interpretation can change).
- Performance: replaying millions of events is slow without snapshots.
- Complexity: developers have to think in events, not state mutations.
- Eventual consistency between command and query side.

sections.title: When to Use Event Sourcing (and When Not To)
sections.content:
**Use ES when:**
- Domain has natural events (order lifecycle, account ledger, document edits).
- Temporal queries are core ('what did this account look like on Dec 31?').
- Audit history must be perfect and queryable (banking, healthcare, accounting).
- Multiple read views are derived from the same data.
- Undo/redo or event replay is a feature.

**Don't use ES when:**
- Simple CRUD on entities with no historical interest (a settings table).
- Performance-critical path with no time for projection lag.
- Team unfamiliar with the pattern — the learning curve is steep and mistakes are expensive.
- Schema is unstable (frequent breaking changes; event versioning becomes a nightmare).

**Pragmatic middle ground:**
- Use **rich audit logging** (the architecture above) for most systems — captures history without taking ES's complexity.
- Reserve full ES for the bounded contexts that genuinely need it (a payments ledger, an order workflow), not the whole app.

sections.title: ES Implementation Details — Snapshots, Projections, Versioning
Failure Modes
sections.content:
**Audit pipeline lag.**
- Outbox grows; alert if backlog > N minutes.
- Add scaling for the outbox-publisher worker.

**Indexer falls behind.**
- Search returns stale results.
- Show 'last indexed at: timestamp' in the audit UI; users know what they're seeing.

**Hash chain break (tamper or bug).**
- Periodic verification job recomputes hashes; alerts on mismatch.
- Investigate; legal review if real tampering.

**Storage growth.**
- Audit logs accumulate; tier old data to cheap storage (S3 Glacier).
- Honor retention policy: delete (or anonymize) after the legal minimum.

**ES-specific: projection corruption.**
- A bug in a projection handler corrupts the read model.
- Fix: drop the read model table, replay events with the corrected handler.
- This is *the* superpower of ES — nothing is lost, just rebuild.

**ES-specific: event schema break.**
- A field was renamed; old events still in the log.
- Fix: upcaster transforms old to new on read; never modify historical events.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Audit log = immutable record of who did what when**, with tamper-evidence (hash chain) and queryable read index.
- **Two stores by design:** append-only cold log (Postgres / S3 / QLDB) + search index (Elasticsearch).
- **Use Outbox or CDC** to write audits reliably without dual-write race.
- **Event Sourcing = events are the source of truth**, not just an audit trail.
- **Use ES for** temporal queries, perfect history, multi-view systems (financial ledgers, order workflows, document editors).
- **Don't use ES for** simple CRUD, fast-evolving schemas, or teams new to the pattern.
- **Snapshots, projections, and event versioning** are the operational backbone of ES.
- **Plain audit logging is enough** for most compliance use cases; full ES is opt-in per bounded context.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Audit log basics**

Append-only record of significant actions: who, what, when, on which object, with what payload, what outcome. Requirements: immutable (no edits), tamper-evident (hash chain or signing), queryable (by user/time/object), retained per policy, performant (must not slow the action being audited).

**The two-store architecture**

Query patterns conflict with append-only storage. So I use two:
- Cold append-only log: Postgres with INSERT-only role, S3 with object lock, AWS QLDB, or Kafka with infinite retention. Source of truth, hash-chained.
- Search index: Elasticsearch denormalized by user/time/target/action. Rebuildable from the cold log.

Queries hit the index; detail clicks fetch the full event by event_id from cold storage.

**Schema essentials**

event_id, occurred_at, recorded_at (skew detection), actor_type/id, action, target_type/id, before_value, after_value, metadata (IP/UA/request-id), outcome, prev_hash, hash.

**Tamper-evidence**

Hash chain: each event's hash = SHA256(prev_hash || payload). Tampering breaks all subsequent hashes. Periodically publish latest hash externally.

For regulated industries: signed events + Merkle root in a notary store. For most enterprise: hash chain + immutable storage is enough.

**Writing reliably — outbox or CDC**

Audit writes must be atomic with the business action. Two patterns:

- Outbox: app writes business change + audit event to its own DB in one transaction; separate worker drains outbox to Kafka. Atomic for business; eventual for audit pipeline.
- CDC (Debezium → Kafka): listen to the WAL; produce automatically. No explicit publish in code.

Never direct dual-write (DB then Kafka separately) — if app crashes between, audit is lost.

**Event Sourcing — the next step**

In ES, the event log IS the source of truth. No current-state table is authoritative; current state is fold(events). Read models (current-state tables) are projections, rebuildable from events.

**Benefits**
- Perfect history — you know exactly what happened and when
- Time travel — reconstruct state at any past moment
- New views for free — project from events
- Bug fixes via replay
- Natural CQRS fit — events are C, projections are Q

**Costs**
- Schema evolution is hard — events are immutable, but interpretation evolves; need upcasters
- Performance — replaying millions of events is slow without snapshots
- Complexity — think in events, not state mutations
- Eventual consistency between command and query

**When to use ES**

Use for:
- Natural-event domains (order lifecycle, account ledger, document edits)
- Temporal queries are core ('what did account X look like on Dec 31?')
- Audit must be perfect (banking, healthcare, accounting)
- Multiple read views from same data
- Undo/redo as a feature

Don't use for:
- Simple CRUD with no history
- Performance-critical paths sensitive to projection lag
- Teams new to the pattern (steep curve, expensive mistakes)
- Unstable schemas (event versioning becomes a nightmare)

Pragmatic middle ground: rich audit logging for most things; full ES only for bounded contexts that genuinely need it (the payments ledger, the order workflow).

**ES implementation details**

Snapshots: replay millions of events is slow; periodically snapshot current state, replay only events since the snapshot.

Projections: subscribers consume events, update denormalized read stores. Each projection is independent and rebuildable from the log.

Event versioning: events are immutable but understanding evolves. Use upcasters — functions transforming old event versions to new at read time. Or versioned event types (OrderCreatedV1, V2). Never edit historical events.

Idempotent handlers: projections might re-process; upsert keyed by event_id.

Tooling: EventStoreDB, Marten, Axon Framework handle snapshots / projections / versioning out of the box.

**Failure handling**

- Outbox lag: alert if backlog > N minutes; scale workers
- Indexer lag: show 'last indexed at' in audit UI
- Hash chain break: periodic verification job; alert on mismatch
- Storage growth: tier to S3 Glacier; honor retention policy
- ES projection corruption: drop the table, replay with fixed handler — this is THE superpower
- ES schema break: upcaster transforms; never modify history

**Recommendation**

**For most systems: rich audit logging — immutable append-only log (Postgres/S3/QLDB) + Elasticsearch index, written reliably via outbox or CDC, hash-chained for tamper evidence. Reserve full Event Sourcing for bounded contexts where temporal queries, perfect history, or multiple read models are the value (financial ledgers, complex workflows). Plain audit logging covers 90% of compliance and security forensics needs without taking on ES complexity. When you do reach for ES, lean on snapshots, design for upcasters from day one, and use battle-tested tooling like EventStoreDB or Axon.**

questions.question: Design an in-process pub/sub event bus in Java. How do you handle type safety, async delivery, and subscriber lifecycle?
questions.title: Design a Pub/Sub Event Bus in Java
questions.direct_answer: Index subscribers by **`Class<? extends Event>`** so dispatch is **`Map<Class, List<Handler>>`**. Use **`CopyOnWriteArrayList`** for handler lists (read-mostly, rare subscribe) and an **`ExecutorService`** for async delivery. Hold subscribers via **`WeakReference`** to avoid leaking memory when callers forget to unsubscribe. Isolate failures (one handler throwing must not kill others) and **never block the publish thread** by default. The popular references: **Guava's EventBus** for simple in-process, **Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher**, **Vert.x EventBus** for clustered, **LMAX Disruptor** for ultra-low-latency.

interviewer_intent.testing: Subscriber registry data structure, type-safe dispatch, async delivery model, failure isolation, and lifecycle management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Synchronous in-thread delivery (one slow handler blocks all), strong references holding subscribers forever, or no per-handler error isolation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss back-pressure (bounded queue), ordering guarantees (per topic/per key), Disruptor's ring-buffer alternative for ultra-low-latency, and dead-event handling for unhandled types.

sections.title: What the Event Bus Must Do
sections.content:
API:
- `subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> handler)` — register interest in events of a type.
- `unsubscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<E> handler)` — remove a subscriber.
- `publish(Event e)` — dispatch to all handlers registered for `e.getClass()` (and parent types if hierarchy is supported).

Non-functional:
- **Type-safe** — a handler for `OrderShipped` should only receive `OrderShipped` events.
- **Async by default** — publish returns immediately; handlers run on a worker pool.
- **Failure isolated** — one handler's exception must not affect siblings or the publisher.
- **Memory-safe** — unsubscribed (or GC'd) handlers must be reclaimable.
- **Concurrent** — publish and subscribe can race safely.

This is exactly the shape of Google Guava's `EventBus`, Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher`, and Vert.x's `EventBus`. We're rebuilding what's been refined for years.

sections.title: Core Data Structure — Type-Indexed Handler Registry
sections.content:
**Index by event class:**

```java
Map<Class<?>, List<Handler<?>>> handlers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
```

**Why:** dispatch is `handlers.get(event.getClass())`. O(1) lookup. Adding a handler is O(1) amortized.

**Why `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for the inner list:**
- Subscribe/unsubscribe is rare (mostly at startup); publish is hot.
- COWAL gives lock-free reads (just a volatile-array read) at the cost of expensive writes.
- Perfect read-mostly access pattern.

**Subscribing to parent types (Guava-style hierarchy):**
- If `OrderShipped extends OrderEvent`, a handler for `OrderEvent` should also receive `OrderShipped`.
- On publish, walk the class hierarchy of the event and invoke handlers at each level.
- Cache the type chain per event class to avoid re-walking on every publish.

**For maximum simplicity (no hierarchy):**
- Match exactly on `event.getClass()`. Cleaner semantics; what you publish is what subscribers see.

sections.title: LLD — Class Design
Implementation — Async Dispatch with Failure Isolation
Sync vs Async vs Hybrid Dispatch
sections.content:
**Sync dispatch (in publish thread):**
- Pros: no thread-context overhead; easier debugging; ordering is trivial.
- Cons: slow handler blocks publisher; one handler's exception can propagate (mitigate with try/catch).
- Use for: in-process events where handlers are fast and predictable, like Spring's default `ApplicationEventPublisher`.

**Async dispatch (executor pool):**
- Pros: publisher returns immediately; failure isolation natural; concurrent handlers.
- Cons: lose strict ordering (events may execute out of submission order across handlers); thread-context cost.
- Use for: handlers may be slow, IO-bound, or many.

**Hybrid:** sync per-handler order with parallelism across distinct events.
- Per-handler single-threaded executor; events for one handler queue in order.
- Different handlers progress in parallel.
- LMAX Disruptor takes this further with a ring buffer and gated consumers.

**Bounded queue is critical:**
- Unbounded executor queue → OOM under load.
- Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` with bounded queue + rejection policy (`CallerRunsPolicy` for backpressure, `AbortPolicy` if dropping is acceptable).

sections.title: Lifecycle — Weak References and Auto-Cleanup
sections.content:
**Problem:** subscriber object goes out of scope but bus still references it — memory leak.

**Solution: weak references.**

```java
record WeakHandler<E>(WeakReference<Consumer<E>> ref) {
    Optional<Consumer<E>> resolve() { return Optional.ofNullable(ref.get()); }
}
```

On publish, check `resolve()`; if null (GC'd), remove the handler.

**Caveats:**
- Lambdas capture their enclosing instance — the lambda itself is held by the registry, but it transitively holds the capturer.
- Best practice: explicit `unsubscribe`/`Subscription.cancel()`. Weak references are a safety net, not a substitute.

**Auto-cleanup pattern:**
- Tie subscription lifecycle to the subscriber object via `try-with-resources` if the API supports it.
- Spring's `@PreDestroy` and `DisposableBean` for managed beans.
- Manual `close()` in tests.

**For long-lived global subscribers:** strong references are fine; document the lifetime expectation.

sections.title: Ordering and Backpressure
sections.content:
**Ordering guarantees:**

- **Per-handler order** (events arrive at one handler in publication order): use a per-handler single-threaded executor or a sequenced queue.
- **Total order** (all handlers see events in the same order): expensive; serialize publish via a single dispatcher thread.
- **No order guarantee:** the cheapest; default of most async buses.

**Per-key ordering** (events with the same key handled in order):
- Hash key to one of N executors.
- All events with the same key go to the same executor → in order.
- Different keys process in parallel.
- This is exactly Kafka's partition model, in-process.

**Backpressure:**
- Producer outpaces consumers → queue grows.
- Bounded queue + rejection policy:
  - `CallerRunsPolicy`: producer thread runs the task itself → natural backpressure.
  - `AbortPolicy`: drop and throw; useful for non-critical events.
- Monitor queue depth; alert if sustained > threshold.

**LMAX Disruptor pattern:**
- Pre-allocated ring buffer; producers write into slots, consumers read in order.
- Lock-free; bounded throughput limited only by slowest consumer.
- Used for ultra-low-latency event processing (financial trading).

sections.title: Failure Modes
sections.content:
**Handler exception**
- Per-handler try/catch swallows + logs; doesn't affect siblings.
- Optional: send to a poison-event queue for inspection.

**Slow handler causing queue saturation**
- Bounded queue + monitoring of queue depth.
- Per-handler executor isolates; one slow handler doesn't starve others.

**Publisher faster than consumers (sustained)**
- Backpressure via `CallerRunsPolicy` slows the publisher.
- Or drop oldest events (bounded buffer with overwrite semantics) if the data is replaceable (sensor readings).

**Dead events (no subscribers)**
- Record to dead-event queue.
- Useful for catching forgotten subscriptions in dev; aggregate metrics in prod.

**Subscriber leak**
- Weak references catch GC'd subscribers; periodic sweep of broken weak refs in registry.

**Publisher in subscriber (re-entrant publish)**
- Risky if sync dispatch — stack overflow on cycles.
- Async dispatch breaks the cycle by nature.

**Lost events on shutdown**
- Graceful shutdown: stop accepting new events, drain executor queue with timeout, then force-stop.
- For durable delivery, use a real broker (Kafka), not an in-process bus.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Type-indexed registry:** `Map<Class<?>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<?>>>`. Lock-free read.
- **Async dispatch via `ExecutorService`** — publisher returns immediately; per-handler failure isolated by try/catch.
- **Bounded queue + rejection policy** for backpressure; never unbounded.
- **`WeakReference` to subscribers** as a leak safety net; explicit `unsubscribe` is the contract.
- **Per-key ordering** via hash-to-executor (Kafka-partition model in-process).
- **Dead-event queue** captures unhandled events for debugging.
- **In production, use Guava's EventBus, Spring's events, Vert.x EventBus, or LMAX Disruptor** — don't roll your own unless requirements are unusual.
- **In-process bus is not durable** — use Kafka/RabbitMQ if events must survive process restart.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The data structure**

Map from event Class to a list of handlers. ConcurrentHashMap outer; CopyOnWriteArrayList for the inner list. Subscribe and unsubscribe are rare; publish is hot — COWAL gives lock-free reads (just a volatile array read) at the cost of expensive writes. Perfect read-mostly fit.

Dispatch is `registry.get(event.getClass())` — O(1) lookup, then iterate handlers.

**Hierarchy support — optional**

If events extend a base type and parents should receive child events too, walk the class hierarchy on publish. Cache the type chain per event class. For maximum simplicity, exact-class match — cleaner semantics.

**Async dispatch**

Publisher returns immediately; handlers run on an ExecutorService. Why:
- Slow handlers don't block publisher
- Failure isolation natural — wrap each handler in try/catch in the executor task
- Handlers run concurrently

Trade-off: lose strict cross-handler ordering. Sync is simpler if handlers are fast and predictable (Spring's default).

**Per-handler failure isolation**

```java
for (Handler<?> h : targets) {
    executor.submit(() -> {
        try { ((Handler<E>) h).accept(event); }
        catch (Throwable t) { log.error(...); }
    });
}
```

One handler throwing doesn't affect siblings or the publisher.

**Subscription lifecycle**

Return a Subscription handle from `subscribe()`; caller calls `cancel()` to unsubscribe. Cleaner than passing the consumer back.

Memory safety: WeakReference to subscriber as a safety net for forgotten unsubscribes. But: lambdas capture enclosing instances, so explicit unsubscribe is still the contract. Spring's @PreDestroy / DisposableBean for managed beans.

**Ordering and per-key ordering**

Default async dispatch loses cross-event ordering. If per-handler order matters, use a per-handler single-threaded executor.

For per-key ordering (events with same key handled in order, different keys in parallel): hash key to one of N executors. Same key → same executor → in order. Same model as Kafka partitions, but in-process.

**Backpressure**

Critical: bounded queue. Unbounded executor queue = OOM under load.

- CallerRunsPolicy: publisher thread runs the task itself — natural backpressure
- AbortPolicy: drop and throw if dropping is acceptable
- Monitor queue depth; alert if sustained > threshold

LMAX Disruptor pattern: pre-allocated ring buffer with lock-free producers/consumers; ultra-low-latency for financial trading.

**Dead events**

Events with no subscribers: record to a dead-event queue. Catches forgotten subscriptions in dev; aggregate metrics in prod.

**LLD**

- EventBus facade with subscribe/unsubscribe/publish
- HandlerRegistry: type-indexed map operations
- Dispatcher interface: SyncDispatcher / AsyncDispatcher / DisruptorDispatcher — swappable
- DeadEventQueue
- Subscription returned for clean unsubscribe

**Failure modes**

- Handler exception — per-handler try/catch swallows + logs; optional poison-event queue
- Slow handler — bounded queue; per-handler executor isolates
- Sustained over-publish — backpressure via CallerRunsPolicy or drop-oldest
- Subscriber leak — WeakReference safety net + periodic sweep
- Re-entrant publish (handler publishes) — risky in sync; async breaks cycles
- Lost events on shutdown — graceful drain with timeout; for durability use Kafka

**Production choices**

- Guava EventBus — simple in-process
- Spring ApplicationEventPublisher — integrated with bean lifecycle
- Vert.x EventBus — supports clustered (cross-process)
- LMAX Disruptor — ultra-low-latency ring buffer

**Recommendation**

**For most in-process use: Map<Class, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler>> as registry, ExecutorService with bounded queue for async dispatch, per-handler try/catch for failure isolation, Subscription handle for explicit unsubscribe with WeakReference as safety net. For per-key ordering, hash to one of N single-threaded executors. In production, prefer Guava EventBus or Spring events over rolling your own; reach for LMAX Disruptor only when you genuinely need microsecond latencies. For events that must survive restart, use a real broker like Kafka or RabbitMQ — in-process buses are not durable.**
